question: What is IPC Section 420?
answer: IPC Section 420 deals with cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property. Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person or to make alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine.

question: What is IPC Section 302?
answer: IPC Section 302 prescribes punishment for murder. Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life and shall also be liable to fine.

question: What is IPC Section 376?
answer: IPC Section 376 deals with punishment for rape. It prescribes rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than ten years which may extend to imprisonment for life and shall also be liable to fine.

question: What is IPC Section 498A?
answer: IPC Section 498A deals with husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty. Whoever being the husband or the relative of the husband of a woman subjects such woman to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine.

question: What is IPC Section 406?
answer: IPC Section 406 deals with criminal breach of trust. Whoever commits criminal breach of trust shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years or with fine or with both.

question: What is IPC Section 304B?
answer: IPC Section 304B deals with dowry death. Where the death of a woman is caused by any burns or bodily injury or occurs otherwise than under normal circumstances within seven years of her marriage and it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband for or in connection with any demand for dowry such death shall be called dowry death.

question: What is IPC Section 354?
answer: IPC Section 354 deals with assault or criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty. Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any woman intending to outrage or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby outrage her modesty shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to five years and shall also be liable to fine.

question: What is IPC Section 379?
answer: IPC Section 379 deals with punishment for theft. Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years or with fine or with both.

question: What is IPC Section 323?
answer: IPC Section 323 deals with punishment for voluntarily causing hurt. Whoever except in the case provided for by section 334 voluntarily causes hurt shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees or with both.

question: What is IPC Section 506?
answer: IPC Section 506 deals with punishment for criminal intimidation. Whoever commits the offence of criminal intimidation shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years or with fine or with both.

question: What is IPC Section 307?
answer: IPC Section 307 deals with attempt to murder. Whoever does any act with such intention or knowledge and under such circumstances that if he by that act caused death he would be guilty of murder shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years and shall also be liable to fine.

question: What is IPC Section 467?
answer: IPC Section 467 deals with forgery of valuable security will etc. Whoever forges a document which purports to be a valuable security or a will or an authority to adopt a son or which purports to give authority to any person to make or transfer any valuable security shall be punished with imprisonment for life or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years and shall also be liable to fine.

question: What is IPC Section 468?
answer: IPC Section 468 deals with forgery for purpose of cheating. Whoever commits forgery intending that the document or electronic record forged shall be used for the purpose of cheating shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine.

question: What is IPC Section 34?
answer: IPC Section 34 deals with acts done by several persons in furtherance of common intention. When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone.

question: What is Article 14 of the Indian Constitution?
answer: Article 14 guarantees equality before the law - The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. It prohibits discrimination on the basis of religion race caste sex or place of birth.

question: What is Article 19 of the Indian Constitution?
answer: Article 19 protects six fundamental freedoms: (a) freedom of speech and expression (b) freedom to assemble peaceably and without arms (c) freedom to form associations or unions (d) freedom to move freely throughout the territory of India (e) freedom to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India (f) freedom to practise any profession or to carry on any occupation trade or business.

question: What is Article 21 of the Indian Constitution?
answer: Article 21 states that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. This article has been given the widest possible interpretation by the Supreme Court of India to include the right to live with dignity right to livelihood right to health right to education right to shelter right to privacy and many other rights.

question: What is Article 32 of the Indian Constitution?
answer: Article 32 provides the right to constitutional remedies. It empowers citizens to move the Supreme Court for the enforcement of fundamental rights. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called it the soul and heart of the Constitution. The Supreme Court can issue writs including habeas corpus mandamus prohibition certiorari and quo warranto.

question: What is Article 226 of the Indian Constitution?
answer: Article 226 empowers every High Court to issue writs including habeas corpus mandamus prohibition certiorari and quo warranto for the enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose. The power of the High Court under Article 226 is wider than that of the Supreme Court under Article 32.

question: What is Article 15 of the Indian Constitution?
answer: Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion race caste sex or place of birth. The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on these grounds. No citizen shall be subjected to any disability liability restriction or condition with regard to access to shops public restaurants hotels and places of public entertainment or the use of wells tanks bathing ghats roads and places of public resort.

question: What is Article 370 of the Indian Constitution?
answer: Article 370 was a temporary provision granting special autonomous status to Jammu and Kashmir. It was abrogated on August 5 2019 by a Presidential Order effectively revoking the special status of Jammu and Kashmir. The state was reorganized into two Union Territories: Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.

question: What is Article 44 of the Indian Constitution?
answer: Article 44 is a Directive Principle of State Policy that states the State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of India. It aims to have one common law for all citizens regardless of their religion in matters of personal law such as marriage divorce inheritance and adoption.

question: What are fundamental rights in India?
answer: Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution (Articles 12-35). There are six fundamental rights: (1) Right to Equality (Articles 14-18) (2) Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22) (3) Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24) (4) Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28) (5) Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30) (6) Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32).

question: What is a writ petition in India?
answer: A writ petition is a formal written request to a court asking it to issue a writ or order. In India writ petitions can be filed under Article 32 (Supreme Court) or Article 226 (High Court). The five types of writs are: Habeas Corpus (produce the body) Mandamus (command to perform duty) Prohibition (prohibit lower court) Certiorari (quash order of lower court) and Quo Warranto (by what authority).

question: What is Section 125 CrPC?
answer: Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure deals with maintenance of wives children and parents. If any person having sufficient means neglects or refuses to maintain his wife unable to maintain herself or his legitimate or illegitimate minor child or his father or mother unable to maintain themselves a Magistrate may order such person to pay a monthly allowance for their maintenance.

question: What is Section 144 CrPC?
answer: Section 144 CrPC empowers a District Magistrate Sub-Divisional Magistrate or any Executive Magistrate to issue an order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger. The order can direct any person to abstain from a certain act or to take certain order with respect to certain property. This section is commonly used to impose curfew or prohibit assembly of people.

question: What is Section 154 CrPC?
answer: Section 154 CrPC deals with the First Information Report (FIR). Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence if given orally to an officer in charge of a police station shall be reduced to writing by him or under his direction and the substance thereof shall be entered in a book. A copy of the FIR shall be given to the informant free of cost.

question: What is Section 156(3) CrPC?
answer: Section 156(3) CrPC empowers a Magistrate to order an investigation by the police. If the police refuse to register an FIR the aggrieved person can approach the Magistrate under this section who can then direct the police to investigate and register the FIR. This is an important remedy when police refuse to act.

question: What is anticipatory bail?
answer: Anticipatory bail is a direction to release a person on bail issued even before the person is arrested. It is granted under Section 438 of CrPC. A person who apprehends that he may be arrested on an accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction that in the event of such arrest he shall be released on bail.

question: What is bail in Indian law?
answer: Bail is the release of a person from legal custody by providing surety for their appearance. In Indian law offences are categorized as bailable and non-bailable. In bailable offences bail is a matter of right under Section 436 CrPC. In non-bailable offences bail is at the discretion of the court under Section 437 CrPC.

question: What is the Indian Contract Act?
answer: The Indian Contract Act 1872 is the main law governing contracts in India. It defines and regulates contracts under Indian law. Key provisions include: offer and acceptance (Section 2) consideration (Section 2d) free consent (Section 14) void and voidable contracts (Sections 2g and 2i) performance of contracts (Section 37) and breach of contract remedies (Section 73).

question: What is Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act?
answer: Section 27 declares that every agreement by which anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful profession trade or business of any kind is to that extent void. This makes non-compete clauses in employment contracts largely unenforceable in India as they are considered agreements in restraint of trade.

question: What is consideration in contract law?
answer: Under Section 2(d) of the Indian Contract Act consideration is defined as when at the desire of the promisor the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing or does or abstains from doing or promises to do or to abstain from doing something such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the promise. A contract without consideration is void under Section 25.

question: What makes a contract void?
answer: Under Indian Contract Act a contract is void if: (1) it involves unlawful consideration or object (Section 23) (2) it restrains trade (Section 27) (3) it restrains legal proceedings (Section 28) (4) the meaning is uncertain (Section 29) (5) it is a wagering agreement (Section 30) (6) it is entered by a minor or person of unsound mind (Section 11-12) (7) consent is obtained by coercion undue influence fraud or misrepresentation.

question: What is breach of contract?
answer: Breach of contract occurs when one party fails to fulfill their obligations under the contract. Under Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act the aggrieved party is entitled to receive compensation for any loss or damage caused by the breach. The compensation cannot exceed what the parties knew when they made the contract to be likely to result from the breach.

question: What is the Consumer Protection Act 2019?
answer: The Consumer Protection Act 2019 replaced the earlier 1986 Act and provides enhanced protection to consumers. Key features include: establishment of Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) provisions for product liability mediation as alternate dispute resolution mechanism provisions for e-commerce consumers and penalties for misleading advertisements.

question: How to file a consumer complaint?
answer: To file a consumer complaint: (1) Write a complaint with details of the product/service defects amount claimed and documents (2) File at the appropriate forum based on the value of goods: District Commission for claims up to Rs 1 crore State Commission for Rs 1-10 crore National Commission for above Rs 10 crore (3) You can also file online at edaakhil.nic.in. No advocate is mandatory.

question: What is product liability?
answer: Under the Consumer Protection Act 2019 product liability means the responsibility of a product manufacturer product seller or product service provider to compensate for any harm caused to a consumer by a defective product or deficiency in services. A product liability action can be brought by a complainant against a product manufacturer product seller or product service provider.

question: What are unfair trade practices?
answer: Unfair trade practices under the Consumer Protection Act include: false representation about quality standard grade composition style or model of goods misleading advertisements selling goods not conforming to product safety standards manufacturing spurious goods and not issuing bills or receipts for goods sold or services rendered.

question: What is the Rent Control Act?
answer: Rent Control Acts are state-level laws in India that regulate the relationship between landlords and tenants. Key provisions include: fixing fair rent preventing unreasonable eviction of tenants regulating rent increases providing for maintenance and repairs and establishing rent courts for dispute resolution. Each state has its own rent control legislation.

question: What are tenant rights in India?
answer: Tenants in India have the following rights: (1) Right to fair rent as determined by rent control authorities (2) Right against illegal eviction without proper notice and due process (3) Right to essential services like water electricity etc. (4) Right to have the property maintained in habitable condition (5) Right to have security deposit returned after deducting legitimate expenses (6) Right to privacy with proper notice before landlord entry.

question: Can a landlord increase rent arbitrarily?
answer: No a landlord cannot increase rent arbitrarily. Under most state rent control acts: rent can only be increased at the rate specified in the rental agreement. In rent-controlled areas increases are capped by law usually 5-10% per year. The landlord must give proper written notice (usually 30-90 days) before any increase. If the increase is unreasonable tenants can approach the Rent Controller.

question: What is the 11-month rental agreement trap?
answer: The 11-month rental agreement is a common legal tactic used by landlords in India. Under the Registration Act 1908 any lease agreement for more than 1 year must be registered with the Sub-Registrar and attracts stamp duty. To avoid this cost and legal obligations landlords create Leave and License agreements for exactly 11 months. This effectively strips tenants of protections offered by Rent Control Acts since these acts typically apply only to registered leases.

question: What is wrongful termination?
answer: Wrongful termination refers to an employee being fired in violation of legal provisions or the terms of their employment contract. An employee can be wrongfully terminated if: they are fired without proper notice as per the contract they are terminated for discriminatory reasons (caste religion gender etc.) they are fired in retaliation for filing complaints or the termination violates labor law provisions.

question: Are non-compete clauses valid in India?
answer: Non-compete clauses after termination of employment are generally not enforceable in India. Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act 1872 declares every agreement in restraint of trade void. Indian courts have consistently held that non-compete clauses that restrict an employee from working after leaving a company are unenforceable. However non-compete during employment and non-solicitation clauses may be enforceable if reasonable.

question: What is the Payment of Wages Act?
answer: The Payment of Wages Act 1936 regulates the payment of wages to certain classes of employed persons. Key provisions: wages must be paid before the 7th or 10th of the month depending on establishment size. Deductions from wages are limited and regulated. Workers can file complaints for delayed or non-payment of wages before the authority appointed under the Act.

question: What is POSH Act?
answer: The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention Prohibition and Redressal) Act 2013 commonly known as the POSH Act mandates that every employer with 10 or more employees must constitute an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) for redressal of sexual harassment complaints. The act covers all women regardless of their age or employment status.

question: What is the Domestic Violence Act?
answer: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 provides protection to women from domestic violence. It covers physical abuse sexual abuse verbal and emotional abuse and economic abuse. An aggrieved woman can file a complaint before a Magistrate and seek protection orders residence orders monetary relief custody orders and compensation orders.
source: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005

question: What is the Hindu Marriage Act?
answer: The Hindu Marriage Act 1955 codifies the law relating to marriage among Hindus. Key provisions include: conditions for a valid Hindu marriage (Section 5) registration of marriages ceremonies for Hindu marriages grounds for divorce (Section 13) including cruelty desertion conversion unsoundness of mind and incurable disease. Mutual consent divorce is available under Section 13B.

question: What are grounds for divorce in India?
answer: Grounds for divorce under Hindu Marriage Act include: (1) Adultery (2) Cruelty (3) Desertion for a continuous period of not less than two years (4) Conversion to another religion (5) Unsoundness of mind (6) Leprosy (7) Venereal disease (8) Renunciation of the world (9) Not heard of as being alive for seven years. Mutual consent divorce is available under Section 13B after one year of separation.

question: What is the Right to Information Act?
answer: The Right to Information Act 2005 (RTI) mandates timely response to citizen requests for government information. Any citizen can request information from a public authority which must reply within 30 days. The Act covers all constitutional authorities including the executive legislature and judiciary. There are penalties for delay or denial of information up to Rs 250 per day of delay.

question: What is a legal notice?
answer: A legal notice is a formal communication sent by one party to another informing them of their intention to take legal action if their demand is not met. Under Section 80 of CPC a two-month notice must be given before filing a suit against the government. Legal notices are usually sent through registered post or speed post and should contain: facts of the case relief sought and time limit for compliance.

question: What is an FIR?
answer: A First Information Report (FIR) is a written document prepared by the police when they receive information about the commission of a cognizable offence. It is filed under Section 154 of CrPC. Key points: It can be filed by anyone not necessarily the victim. Police are obligated to register an FIR for cognizable offences. If police refuse to file an FIR you can send the complaint by registered post to the SP or file a complaint before a Magistrate under Section 156(3) CrPC.

question: What is cyber crime in India?
answer: Cyber crimes in India are dealt with under the Information Technology Act 2000 and Indian Penal Code. Common cyber crimes include: hacking (Section 66 IT Act) identity theft (Section 66C) cheating by personation (Section 66D) sending offensive messages (Section 66A struck down) cyber stalking (Section 354D IPC) publishing obscene material (Section 67 IT Act). Complaints can be filed at cybercrime.gov.in or the local police station.

question: What is the Motor Vehicles Act?
answer: The Motor Vehicles Act 1988 regulates all aspects of road transport vehicles. Key provisions include: licensing and registration of motor vehicles regulation of transport vehicles special provisions relating to accidents and liability insurance coverage for third-party risks and penalties for traffic offences. The 2019 amendment significantly increased penalties for traffic violations.

question: What is a Power of Attorney?
answer: A Power of Attorney (POA) is a legal document where one person (the principal) authorizes another person (the agent or attorney) to act on their behalf. Types include: General Power of Attorney (broad authority) Special Power of Attorney (specific tasks) Durable Power of Attorney (continues even if principal becomes incapacitated). A POA must be executed on stamp paper and can be registered for added legal validity.

question: What is RERA?
answer: The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act 2016 (RERA) was enacted to protect homebuyers and regulate the real estate sector. Key features: all commercial and residential projects with area above 500 sq meters or 8 apartments must be registered. Developers must deposit 70% of funds in a separate account. Buyers can file complaints with RERA authorities for delays defects or violations.

question: What is stamp duty?
answer: Stamp duty is a tax levied by the state government on the execution of legal documents such as sale deeds lease deeds gift deeds and mortgage deeds. The rate varies from state to state typically ranging from 3% to 8% of the property value. Non-payment or insufficient payment of stamp duty can make the document inadmissible as evidence in court.

question: What is arbitration in India?
answer: Arbitration is an alternative dispute resolution mechanism governed by the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996. It allows parties to resolve disputes outside the court system through a neutral third party (arbitrator). The arbitral award is final and binding. Key features: parties can choose their arbitrator the process is confidential and faster than litigation and the award is enforceable like a court decree.

question: What is cheque bounce law?
answer: Cheque bounce is an offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881. If a cheque is dishonoured due to insufficient funds the payee can file a complaint within 30 days of receiving the memo from the bank. The drawer must first send a demand notice within 30 days of dishonour. If payment is not made within 15 days of receipt of notice the payee can file a criminal complaint. Punishment includes imprisonment up to two years and fine up to twice the cheque amount.

question: What is GST?
answer: GST (Goods and Services Tax) is a comprehensive indirect tax levied on the supply of goods and services in India since July 1 2017. It replaced multiple indirect taxes. GST has four slabs: 5% 12% 18% and 28%. Key features: input tax credit is available to avoid cascading taxes. Anti-profiteering provisions ensure businesses pass on the benefits of tax reduction to consumers.

question: What is the difference between cognizable and non-cognizable offences?
answer: Cognizable offences are serious offences where the police can arrest without a warrant and can start investigation without the order of a Magistrate (e.g. murder theft robbery). Non-cognizable offences are relatively less serious offences where the police cannot arrest without a warrant and cannot investigate without the permission of a Magistrate (e.g. assault defamation cheating).

question: What is sedition law in India?
answer: Sedition is defined under Section 124A of the Indian Penal Code. It criminalizes any words written or spoken or signs or visible representation that bring or attempt to bring into hatred or contempt or excite or attempt to excite disaffection towards the Government. The Supreme Court in 2022 effectively put Section 124A on hold directing the government to re-examine the colonial-era provision.

question: What is defamation law in India?
answer: Defamation in India can be both a civil wrong and a criminal offence. Criminal defamation is punishable under Sections 499 and 500 of the IPC with imprisonment up to two years and/or fine. Civil defamation allows the aggrieved person to sue for damages. Truth is a defence to defamation if it is published for the public good. The Supreme Court upheld the validity of criminal defamation in 2016.

question: What is the Limitation Act?
answer: The Limitation Act 1963 prescribes time limits within which a person must file a suit or appeal. Key limitation periods: 3 years for recovery of money or movable property 12 years for recovery of immovable property 30 days for filing appeal in most cases. Filing a case beyond the prescribed limitation period results in the case being time-barred unless the court condones the delay.

question: What is POCSO Act?
answer: The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act 2012 (POCSO) is a special law to protect children below 18 years from sexual abuse and exploitation. It defines various types of sexual offences against children and prescribes stringent punishments. Key features: child-friendly procedures for recording evidence and trial establishment of special courts mandatory reporting of offences and time-bound trial completion.

question: What is the SC/ST Atrocities Act?
answer: The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989 prevents atrocities against members of SC and ST communities. It lists various offences including: forcing to eat inedible substances wrongful dispossession from land compelling bonded labor tampering with drinking water sources and denial of public services. The Act provides for special courts and stringent punishments.

question: What is money laundering?
answer: Money laundering is an offence under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act 2002 (PMLA). It involves disguising the origins of illegally obtained money typically by passing it through a complex sequence of banking transfers or commercial transactions. Punishment includes rigorous imprisonment for 3 to 7 years and fine up to Rs 5 lakh. The Enforcement Directorate (ED) is the primary investigation agency.

question: What is the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code?
answer: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 (IBC) provides a time-bound process for resolving insolvency and bankruptcy. Key features: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) must be completed within 180 days (extendable by 90 days). The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) adjudicates corporate insolvency. Individual insolvency is handled by the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT).

question: What is environmental law in India?
answer: Environmental law in India is governed by multiple acts: Environment Protection Act 1986 Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981 Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974 and National Green Tribunal Act 2010. The National Green Tribunal (NGT) handles environmental disputes. Violations can lead to imprisonment up to 5 years and fine up to Rs 1 lakh or both.

question: What is a non-compete clause?
answer: A non-compete clause is a contractual term that restricts an employee from working with competitors or starting a competing business after leaving the employment. In India such clauses are largely unenforceable after termination of employment as per Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act which declares agreements in restraint of trade as void. However non-compete during employment is generally valid.

question: What is the difference between civil and criminal cases?
answer: Civil cases involve disputes between individuals or organizations where the remedy is usually monetary compensation or specific performance. Criminal cases involve offences against the state or society where the remedy is punishment (imprisonment and/or fine). In civil cases the burden of proof is preponderance of probabilities. In criminal cases the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Civil cases are filed by individuals while criminal cases are filed by the state.

question: What is the penalty for drunk driving in India?
answer: Under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act driving under the influence of drugs or alcohol is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months and/or fine up to Rs 10000 for the first offence. For second offence within 3 years imprisonment up to 2 years and/or fine up to Rs 15000. The 2019 amendment significantly increased these penalties.

question: What is RTI and how to file it?
answer: RTI (Right to Information) can be filed by any Indian citizen under the RTI Act 2005. To file: (1) Write an application on plain paper addressed to the Public Information Officer (PIO) of the relevant government department (2) Pay Rs 10 as application fee (3) Submit via post email or online at rtionline.gov.in. The PIO must respond within 30 days. First appeal can be made within 30 days to the First Appellate Authority.

question: What is the Hindu Succession Act?
answer: The Hindu Succession Act 1956 governs succession and inheritance of property among Hindus Buddhists Jains and Sikhs. The 2005 amendment gave daughters equal coparcenary rights in ancestral property as sons. Key provisions: Class I heirs (including sons daughters mother widow) have priority in succession. A Hindu can dispose of self-acquired property by will.

question: What is maintenance under Hindu law?
answer: Under Section 125 CrPC and the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act 1956 a wife children and parents can claim maintenance. A wife is entitled to maintenance if she is unable to maintain herself. The amount depends on the income of the husband and the reasonable needs of the wife. Interim maintenance can also be granted during the pendency of proceedings.

question: What is medical negligence?
answer: Medical negligence occurs when a medical professional fails to provide the standard of care that a reasonably competent professional would have provided resulting in harm to the patient. Under the Consumer Protection Act 2019 patients can file complaints in consumer courts. The Supreme Court in the Bolam test laid down that a doctor is not negligent if they act in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical men.

question: What is the law on data privacy in India?
answer: India enacted the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 (DPDPA) to protect digital personal data. Key features: citizens have the right to know what data is being collected and for what purpose. Data fiduciaries must obtain consent before collecting personal data. Penalties for data breaches can go up to Rs 250 crore. The Act applies to processing of digital personal data within India or outside India if related to offering goods/services in India.

question: What is the law on property registration?
answer: Under the Indian Registration Act 1908 certain documents must be compulsorily registered including: sale deeds of immovable property leases for more than one year gift deeds of immovable property and powers of attorney authorizing sale of immovable property. Registration must be done at the office of the Sub-Registrar within whose jurisdiction the property is located. Non-registration makes the document inadmissible in evidence.

question: What is an employment bond?
answer: An employment bond is a contract between an employer and employee requiring the employee to serve for a minimum period or pay a specified penalty for early departure. In India employment bonds are governed by the Indian Contract Act 1872. Courts have held that unreasonable employment bonds are void as they violate Section 27 (restraint of trade). However if the employer can prove actual expenditure on training courts may enforce reasonable bond amounts.

question: What is the law on inheritance in India?
answer: Inheritance laws in India differ based on religion. For Hindus Buddhists Jains and Sikhs: governed by the Hindu Succession Act 1956. For Muslims: governed by personal law (Shariat). For Christians and Parsis: governed by the Indian Succession Act 1925. A person can dispose of self-acquired property by will. If a person dies without a will (intestate) the property is distributed according to the applicable succession law.

question: What is land acquisition law?
answer: The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013 (LARR Act) replaced the colonial Land Acquisition Act 1894. Key features: consent of 70-80% of landowners required for acquisition by private entities. Compensation must be at least 2 times the market value in urban areas and 4 times in rural areas. Social impact assessment is mandatory.

question: How much does it cost to consult a lawyer in India?
answer: Lawyer fees in India vary depending on experience and case complexity: (1) Middle Class advocates charge between Rs 12000 and Rs 25000 for standard agreements, rental disputes, or consumer claims. (2) Upper Middle Class advocates charge Rs 18000 to Rs 35000 for property title verification and labor disputes. (3) High Class corporate advocates charge Rs 40000 to Rs 100000+ for commercial litigation and banking fraud.

question: How do I file a police complaint or FIR if police refuse to register it?
answer: If the police refuse to register an FIR: (1) Send your written FIR complaint by Registered Post with Ack Due to the Superintendent of Police (SP) or Commissioner under CrPC Section 154(3). (2) If no action is taken within 15 days, file a private petition before the Judicial Magistrate under CrPC Section 156(3) / BNSS Section 175. The Magistrate can directly order the police to register the FIR and investigate.

question: What is the difference between Consumer Court and Normal Civil Court?
answer: Consumer Court is designed for consumer disputes involving defective products, service deficiencies, GST overcharging, or unfair trade practices. It is faster, cheaper, and accepts online e-filing via edaakhil.nic.in without mandatory lawyer representation. Normal Civil Court handles property title disputes, breach of contracts, loan defaults, and eviction suits governed by the Code of Civil Procedure.

question: What is the landmark Suraj Lamp case study on property title and GPA sale?
answer: In Suraj Lamp & Industries vs State of Haryana (2011), the Supreme Court of India ruled that transfer of immovable property through General Power of Attorney (GPA), Sale Agreement, or Will does not convey lawful title or ownership. The Supreme Court held that immovable property can only be legally transferred through a registered Sale Deed under the Indian Registration Act 1908.

question: What is the Central Inland Water Transport Corp case study on unfair contract terms?
answer: In Central Inland Water Transport Corp vs Brojo Nath Ganguly (1986), the Supreme Court struck down a clause permitting an employer to terminate a permanent employee without cause by giving 3 months notice. The Court ruled that unconscionable, one-sided, oppressive clauses inserted by parties with dominant bargaining power are void under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act as against public policy.

question: What is the Percept DMark case study on non-compete clauses after employment?
answer: In Percept D'Mark (India) Pvt Ltd vs Zaheer Khan (2006), the Supreme Court affirmed that a restrictive covenant extending beyond the term of employment or contract is void and unenforceable under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act 1872. The Court held that freedom of trade and right to livelihood under Article 21 cannot be restricted after contract termination.

question: What is the Satyabrata Ghose case study on contract frustration and Force Majeure?
answer: In Satyabrata Ghose vs Mugneeram Bangur & Co (1954), the Supreme Court laid down the foundation of Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act regarding frustration of contract. The Court held that a contract becomes void if an untoward event or supervening impossibility makes performance of the contract impossible or unlawful, beyond the contemplation of parties.

question: What is the Ram vs Property Dealer case study on hidden rental agreement charges?
answer: In Ram vs Property Dealer (2023), the tenant signed a rental agreement containing buried hidden maintenance charges of Rs 5000 per month. The Civil Court held that hidden clauses not explicitly highlighted during execution constitute unfair misrepresentation under Section 18 of the Indian Contract Act, ordering a full refund of Rs 60000 + Rs 25000 compensation.

question: What is the Sunita vs Electronics Store case study on GST overcharge?
answer: In Sunita vs Electronics Store (2024), a consumer was charged 28% GST on a home appliance instead of the mandatory 18% slab rate. The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission ruled it as an unfair trade practice under Consumer Protection Act 2019, ordering an immediate refund of excess GST along with Rs 10000 punitive compensation.

question: What is the Priya vs Finance Company case study on hidden loan prepayment penalties?
answer: In Priya vs Finance Company (2024), a borrower was subjected to a hidden 5% prepayment penalty buried in fine print when closing a personal loan. Following a complaint to the Banking Ombudsman and Consumer Forum, the tribunal ruled that non-transparent penalty clauses violate RBI Guidelines and Consumer Protection rights, forcing refund of penalty + Rs 15000 costs.

question: What are the court guidance rules for Consumer Court monetary jurisdiction?
answer: Under the Consumer Protection Act 2019: (1) District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission handles claims up to Rs 1 Crore. (2) State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission handles claims between Rs 1 Crore and Rs 10 Crore. (3) National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) handles claims exceeding Rs 10 Crore. Complaints can be filed online via edaakhil.nic.in.

question: What is the court guidance on filing Writ Petitions under Article 226 vs Article 32?
answer: Article 32 allows citizens to approach the Supreme Court directly only for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Certiorari, Prohibition, Quo Warranto) for fundamental rights as well as any other legal right. High Courts have wider territorial and subject-matter writ jurisdiction than the Supreme Court.

question: What is court guidance on e-Filing and online court proceedings in India?
answer: Electronic filing (e-Filing) is enabled across Supreme Court, High Courts, and District Courts via e-filing portals (efiling.ecourts.gov.in). Litigants and advocates can upload digitally signed petitions, pay court fees online via e-Pay, track case status on the eCourts Services app, and attend virtual hearings via video conferencing platforms.

question: What is the court guidance on limitation periods for filing civil suits?
answer: Under the Limitation Act 1963: (1) Suit for breach of contract or recovery of money must be filed within 3 years from the date of cause of action. (2) Suit for possession of immovable property based on title must be filed within 12 years. (3) Appeals to High Court must be filed within 90 days. If delayed, an application for condonation of delay under Section 5 must show sufficient cause.

question: What is court guidance on land registration and encumbrance verification?
answer: Before purchasing immovable property: (1) Verify Patta / Chitta / Settlement records with the State Revenue Department. (2) Obtain an Encumbrance Certificate (EC) for 30+ years from the Sub-Registrar Office to check for existing mortgages, liens, or court attachments. (3) Verify physical survey numbers and boundary measurements against Revenue maps. (4) Ensure property transfer is registered via a public Sale Deed under Section 17 of Registration Act.

question: What is BNS Section 318?
answer: Section 318 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 replaces IPC Section 420 for cheating. Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property shall be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.

question: What is BNS Section 316?
answer: Section 316 of BNS 2023 replaces IPC Section 406 for criminal breach of trust. It punishes anyone who dishonestly misappropriates or converts to their own use property entrusted to them with imprisonment up to 5 years or fine or both.

question: What is BNS Section 336?
answer: Section 336 of BNS 2023 replaces IPC Section 468 for forgery for purpose of cheating. Forging a document or electronic record for cheating carries imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.

question: What is BNS Section 103?
answer: Section 103 of BNS 2023 replaces IPC Section 302 for punishment for murder. It prescribes punishment of death or imprisonment for life, along with fine.

question: What is Section 173 of BNSS?
answer: Section 173 of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) 2023 replaces CrPC Section 154 for First Information Report (FIR). It introduces Zero FIR and allows electronic reporting (e-FIR) for cognizable offences.

question: What is Section 175 of BNSS?
answer: Section 175 of BNSS 2023 replaces CrPC Section 156(3). It empowers a Judicial Magistrate to order a police investigation if the police fail to register an FIR upon written complaint.

question: What is Section 482 of BNSS?
answer: Section 482 of BNSS 2023 replaces CrPC Section 438 for anticipatory bail. A person apprehending arrest in a non-bailable offence may apply to the High Court or Sessions Court for direction to be released on bail in event of arrest.

question: What is BSA Section 61 for electronic evidence?
answer: Section 61 of Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) 2023 governs the admissibility of electronic records. Electronic logs, emails, digital signatures, and mobile records are recognized as primary documentary evidence.

question: What are hidden foreclosure charges in loan documents?
answer: Foreclosure charges are penalties levied by banks or NBFCs when a borrower closes a loan early. Under RBI Guidelines, banks cannot levy foreclosure penalties or prepayment charges on floating-rate home loans or personal loans given to individual borrowers.

question: What is a lock-in period clause in agreement?
answer: A lock-in period clause binds parties to stay in a contract for a minimum duration (e.g., 6 months). If a party exits before the lock-in expires, they may be forced to pay rent/fees for the remainder of the lock-in period. Excessive lock-in penalties without mutual benefit can be challenged in court as oppressive.

question: How to handle unfair deposit deduction by landlord?
answer: If a landlord wrongfully forfeits security deposit: (1) Issue a formal written legal notice demanding refund within 15 days with interest. (2) Show proof of peaceful handover and zero damage beyond normal wear & tear. (3) Approach Small Claims Civil Court or Rent Authority under State Rent Control Act. (4) If commercial lease, file for recovery suit.

question: What is an automatic renewal clause trap?
answer: An automatic renewal clause automatically extends a contract unless a written termination notice is served before a specific deadline. Courts mandate that non-transparent automatic renewals with steep price hikes require explicit prior confirmation, failing which they violate Consumer Protection Act 2019.

question: What is the landmark Kedar Nath case study on public rights?
answer: In Kedar Nath vs State of Bihar (1962), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of sedition but restricted its application strictly to speech or actions that incite imminent violence or public disorder.

question: What is the landmark Navtej Singh Johar case study?
answer: In Navtej Singh Johar vs Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court decriminalized consensual adult samesex relations by reading down Section 377 IPC, holding that fundamental rights under Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21 guarantee bodily autonomy and dignity.

question: What is the landmark Puttaswamy case study on Right to Privacy?
answer: In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy vs Union of India (2017), a 9-judge bench of the Supreme Court unanimously declared the Right to Privacy as a fundamental right intrinsic to life and personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution.

question: வாடகை ஒப்பந்தத்தில் எழும் சிக்கல்களுக்கு தீர்வு என்ன?
answer: வாடகை ஒப்பந்த சிக்கல்களுக்கு: (1) ஒப்பந்த விதிகளை சரிபார்க்கவும். (2) 30 நாட்கள் முன்னறிவிப்புடன் சட்டப்பூர்வ நோட்டீஸ் அனுப்பவும். (3) வைப்புத் தொகை பெற மாநில வாடகை அதிகாரியிடம் (Rent Authority) அல்லது உரிமையியல் நீதிமன்றத்தில் மனு தாக்கல் செய்யலாம்.
source: Tamil Nadu Regulation of Rights and Responsibilities of Landlords and Tenants Act

question: நில பட்டா மற்றும் சிட்டா எவ்வாறு சரிபார்ப்பது?
answer: தமிழக அரசின் eservices.tn.gov.in தளத்தில் மாவட்டம், தாலுகா, கிராமம் மற்றும் பட்டா/புல எண் உள்ளிட்டு உரிமையாளர் பெயர் மற்றும் சொத்தின் பரப்பளவை சரிபார்க்கலாம். வில்லங்க சான்றிதழ் (EC) மூலம் அடமானம் அல்லது கடன் உள்ளதா என்பதை TNREGINET தளத்தில் சரிபார்க்க வேண்டும்.

question: रेंटल एग्रीमेंट में सुरक्षा जमा राशि कैसे वापस पाएं?
answer: यदि मकान मालिक सुरक्षा जमा राशि (Security Deposit) वापस नहीं कर रहा है: (1) 15 दिनों का कानूनी नोटिस भेजें। (2) रेंट अथॉरिटी या उपभोक्ता फोरम में शिकायत दर्ज करें। (3) संपत्ति सौंपने की रसीद और चित्रों को प्रमाण के रूप में सुरक्षित रखें।

question: कंज्यूमर कोर्ट में शिकायत कैसे दर्ज करें?
answer: उपभोक्ता कोर्ट में शिकायत के लिए edaakhil.nic.in पर ऑनलाइन ई-फाइलिंग करें। 1 करोड़ रुपये तक के मामलों के लिए जिला उपभोक्ता आयोग (District Commission) में बिना वकील के भी शिकायत दर्ज की जा सकती है।

question: What is Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act 1905?
answer: The Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act 1905 provides measures for checking unauthorized occupation of government-owned lands (poramboke, water bodies, grazing lands). Under Section 6, the Revenue Tahsildar or authorized officer can issue eviction notices and summarily evict encroachers after summary inquiry. Unauthorized occupants can also be levied penal assessment.

question: What is the Tamil Nadu Patta Pass Book Act 1983?
answer: The Tamil Nadu Patta Pass Book Act 1983 mandates the issuance of Patta Pass Books to landholders. Under Section 3, the Tahsildar issues the Patta Pass Book containing details of landholding, survey number, extent, and tax assessment. Under Section 6, entries in the Patta Pass Book serve as prima facie evidence of title ownership in Tamil Nadu.
source: Tamil Nadu Patta Pass Book Act 1983

question: What is the Tamil Nadu Apartment Ownership Act 2022?
answer: The Tamil Nadu Apartment Ownership Act 2022 regulates ownership of individual apartments and undivided shares (UDS) in common areas. Key features: mandatory formation of apartment owners association, clear statutory definitions of common areas, mandatory registration of association bye-laws with the Sub-Registrar, and streamlined provisions for redevelopment of buildings older than 30 years.

question: What is the Tamil Nadu Cultivating Tenants Protection Act?
answer: The Tamil Nadu Cultivating Tenants Protection Act 1955 protects agricultural tenant farmers against unjust eviction by landlords. Landlords cannot evict a cultivating tenant except for non-payment of rent, doing any act destructive to the land, or willful negligence. Disputes are adjudicated by the Revenue Court (Revenue Divisional Officer).
source: Tamil Nadu Cultivating Tenants Protection Act 1955

question: What is Guideline Value in Tamil Nadu and how is it determined?
answer: Guideline Value in Tamil Nadu is the minimum value fixed by the State Registration Department (TNREGINET) for land and properties in each street or survey number. Stamp duty (typically 7%) and registration fees (2%) are calculated on either the guideline value or the actual sale consideration, whichever is higher. Guideline values are revised periodically by the Valuation Committee.

question: How to verify Patta Chitta online in Tamil Nadu?
answer: To verify Patta Chitta in Tamil Nadu: (1) Visit the official portal eservices.tn.gov.in. (2) Select 'View Patta & FMB / Chitta / TSLR Extract'. (3) Choose District, Taluk, and Village. (4) Enter Patta Number or Survey Number / Sub-division Number. (5) Verify owner name, total area extent, and land classification (Nanjai / Punjai / Natham / Residential).

question: What is an Encumbrance Certificate (EC) in Tamil Nadu?
answer: An Encumbrance Certificate (EC) issued by the Tamil Nadu Registration Department (TNREGINET - tnreginet.gov.in) provides a complete chronological record of all registered property transactions, mortgages, sales, gift deeds, court attachments, and legal claims over a property for a specified period (typically 30 years). A Nil-Encumbrance Certificate indicates a clean title without registered active charges.

question: What is FMB sketch in Tamil Nadu land records?
answer: Field Measurement Book (FMB) is an authentic survey sketch maintained by the Tamil Nadu Survey and Settlement Department. It precisely depicts the exact boundary measurements, sub-division lines, neighboring survey plot numbers, and shape of a specific land parcel. FMB is critical to verify that physical land boundaries match official revenue records.

question: What is the landmark Arnesh Kumar guidelines on police arrest?
answer: In Arnesh Kumar vs State of Bihar (2014), the Supreme Court held that police officers cannot automatically arrest an accused in offences punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years (such as Section 498A IPC). Police must satisfy Section 41 CrPC / Section 35 BNSS conditions and issue a notice of appearance before making an arrest, to prevent arbitrary detentions.
source: Supreme Court of India (2014) - LawSum Dataset

question: What is the landmark D.K. Basu guidelines on arrestee rights?
answer: In D.K. Basu vs State of West Bengal (1997), the Supreme Court laid down 11 mandatory guidelines for arrest and detention to prevent custodial violence: identification badges for police officers, preparation of arrest memo signed by a witness, right of arrestee to inform a relative within 8-12 hours, medical examination every 48 hours, and right to meet a lawyer.
source: Supreme Court of India (1997) - LawSum Dataset

question: What is the landmark Lalita Kumari judgment on mandatory FIR registration?
answer: In Lalita Kumari vs Govt of Uttar Pradesh (2014), a 5-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court ruled that registration of an FIR is mandatory under Section 154 CrPC / Section 173 BNSS if the information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence. Police cannot conduct preliminary inquiry in serious cognizable cases before registering the FIR.
source: Supreme Court of India (2014) - LawSum Dataset

question: What is the landmark Maneka Gandhi case on Article 21 personal liberty?
answer: In Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India (1978), the Supreme Court held that 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 must be just, fair, and reasonable, incorporating the doctrine of substantive Due Process into Indian constitutional jurisprudence. Fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21 form an interconnected golden triangle.
source: Supreme Court of India (1978) - LawSum Dataset

question: What is the landmark Kesavananda Bharati case on Basic Structure?
answer: In Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala (1973), a 13-judge bench of the Supreme Court established the 'Basic Structure Doctrine', ruling that while Parliament has wide power to amend the Constitution under Article 368, it cannot alter or destroy the core basic structure of the Constitution (democracy, rule of law, separation of powers, judicial review).
source: Supreme Court of India (1973) - LawSum Dataset

question: What is the landmark Shayara Bano judgment on Triple Talaq?
answer: In Shayara Bano vs Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court held the practice of Talaq-e-Biddat (instant triple talaq) unconstitutional by a 3:2 majority, finding it arbitrary, discriminatory against Muslim women, and violative of fundamental rights under Article 14 of the Constitution.
source: Supreme Court of India (2017) - ILDC Dataset

question: What is the landmark Vineeta Sharma judgment on daughters coparcenary rights?
answer: In Vineeta Sharma vs Rakesh Sharma (2020), the Supreme Court affirmed that daughters have equal coparcenary rights in ancestral Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) property by birth under the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005, regardless of whether the father was alive when the amendment came into force.
source: Supreme Court of India (2020) - ILDC Dataset

question: What are hidden maintenance charges and how to challenge them?
answer: Hidden maintenance charges are variable costs inserted into rental or commercial agreements that increase total payouts beyond base rent without agreed caps. Under Consumer Protection Act 2019 and Contract Act Section 18, failure to itemize recurring charges upfront constitutes misrepresentation. Tenants can demand itemized audited maintenance bills or contest in Rent Tribunal / Consumer Court.

question: What is a unilateral termination clause in contract law?
answer: A unilateral termination clause allows one dominant party to terminate an agreement without cause or notice while penalizing the other party for exit. Under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act 1872, one-sided clauses resulting from unequal bargaining power that impose disproportionate burdens are unconscionable and void as opposed to public policy.

question: What is an indemnity clause trap in commercial agreements?
answer: An indemnity clause trap requires one party to hold harmless and compensate the other party for any and all third-party claims, legal fees, or regulatory penalties, even when caused by the other party's own negligence. Courts enforce indemnity strictly; parties must negotiate a 'carve-out' for gross negligence, willful misconduct, and cap liability.

question: What is a waiver of subrogation clause in insurance policies?
answer: A waiver of subrogation clause prevents an insurance company from suing a negligent third party to recover claim payouts. While common in commercial lease and construction contracts, policyholders must obtain explicit insurer consent before signing, otherwise the insurer may deny claim coverage for unauthorized waiver of their recovery rights.

question: What are the rules for foreclosure charges by RBI for NBFCs and banks?
answer: Under RBI Master Circulars (2014 & 2019), banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) are strictly prohibited from charging foreclosure fees or prepayment penalties on all floating rate term loans sanctioned to individual borrowers. Fixed rate loans or loans to commercial corporate entities may attract prepayment charges only if explicitly stated in loan sanction terms.

question: What is the Insurance Ombudsman and how to file a claim dispute?
answer: The Insurance Ombudsman is an independent quasi-judicial authority established under the Insurance Ombudsman Rules 2017 to resolve grievances against insurance companies (life, health, motor) up to Rs 30 Lakhs. Complaints can be filed online at ciob.co.in or by post within 1 year of rejection by insurer, without paying any court or advocate fees.

question: What is RERA complaint process for builder delay in property handover?
answer: Under Section 18 of RERA Act 2016, if a promoter fails to give possession of an apartment as per the agreement for sale, the buyer can: (1) Withdraw from the project and demand a full refund of money paid along with prescribed interest (SBI MCLR + 2%). (2) Remain in the project and claim monthly interest for every month of delay until handover. File online via the State RERA portal.

question: What is Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023?
answer: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 replaced the colonial Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860 from July 1, 2024. It consolidates substantive criminal offences into 358 sections, introduces community service as punishment for minor offences, defines organized crime and terrorism, and reorganizes sections (e.g., Section 318 for Cheating, Section 316 for Breach of Trust, Section 103 for Murder).

question: What is Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) 2023?
answer: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) 2023 replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) 1973 from July 1, 2024. Key reforms include: statutory recognition of Zero FIR (Section 173), mandatory electronic recording of search and seizure, forensic investigation mandatory for offences punishable with 7+ years, and strict timelines for judgment delivery within 45 days of trial conclusion.

question: What is Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) 2023?
answer: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) 2023 replaced the Indian Evidence Act 1872 from July 1, 2024. Key provisions: electronic records, digital signatures, server logs, SMS, and messaging apps are given full primary and secondary evidentiary status under Section 61, modernizing court trials for digital evidence without requiring separate archaic certificates in all cases.

question: What is Zero FIR under BNSS Section 173?
answer: A Zero FIR allows any person to register a First Information Report at any police station across India, regardless of jurisdiction or where the crime took place. Under BNSS Section 173(1), the police station must register the complaint immediately under number '0', provide a free copy to the informant, and transfer the case to the competent jurisdictional police station for investigation.

question: தமிழ்நாட்டில் நிலத்தின் வழிகாட்டி மதிப்பு (Guideline Value) என்றால் என்ன?
answer: தமிழ்நாட்டில் பதிவுத் துறையால் (TNREGINET) ஒவ்வொரு தெருவிற்கும் அல்லது புல எண்ணிற்கும் நிர்ணயிக்கப்படும் குறைந்தபட்ச நில மதிப்பு 'வழிகாட்டி மதிப்பு' (Guideline Value) எனப்படும். சொத்து பத்திரப் பதிவின் போது முத்திரைத் தாள் கட்டணம் (7%) மற்றும் பதிவுக் கட்டணம் (2%) வழிகாட்டி மதிப்பு அல்லது உண்மையான விற்பனைத் தொகை இவற்றில் எது அதிகமோ அதன் அடிப்படையில் கணக்கிடப்படும்.

question: வில்லங்கச் சான்றிதழ் (EC) எவ்வாறு பார்ப்பது?
answer: வில்லங்கச் சான்றிதழ் (Encumbrance Certificate) பெற tnreginet.gov.in தளத்திற்குச் செல்லவும்: (1) மண்டலம், மாவட்டம், மற்றும் சார்பதிவாளர் அலுவலகத்தைத் தேர்வு செய்யவும். (2) கிராமம் மற்றும் புல எண் (Survey No) உள்ளிடவும். (3) குறிப்பிட்ட காலத்திற்கு (30 ஆண்டுகள்) சொத்தில் வங்கி அடமானம், விற்பனை, அல்லது நீதிமன்ற வழக்குகள் ஏதேனும் உள்ளதா என சரிபார்க்கலாம். வில்லங்கம் இல்லையெனில் 'Nil Encumbrance' என வரும்.

question: தமிழ்நாட்டில் வாடகை ஒப்பந்த சட்டம் 2017 என்ன கூறுகிறது?
answer: தமிழ்நாடு நில உரிமையாளர்கள் மற்றும் வாடகைதாரர்கள் உரிமைகள் மற்றும் பொறுப்புகள் ஒழுங்குமுறைச் சட்டம் 2017-ன் படி: (1) அனைத்து வாடகை ஒப்பந்தங்களும் எழுத்துப்பூர்வமாக உருவாக்கப்பட்டு வாடகை அதிகாரியிடம் (Rent Authority) பதிவு செய்யப்பட வேண்டும். (2) அதிகபட்ச பாதுகாப்பு வைப்புத் தொகை 3 மாத வாடகைக்கு மிகாமல் இருக்க வேண்டும். (3) சரியான காரணமின்றி வாடகைதாரரை வெளியேற்ற முடியாது.

question: மோசடி ஆவணத்தில் கையெழுத்திட்டால் என்ன செய்ய வேண்டும்?
answer: மோசடியான அல்லது ஆபத்தான சட்ட ஆவணத்தில் கையெழுத்திட்டிருந்தால்: (1) உடனடியாக அருகிலுள்ள காவல் நிலையத்தில் பாரதிய நியாய சன்ஹிதா (BNS) பிரிவு 318 (ஏமாற்றுதல்) மற்றும் பிரிவு 336 (போலி ஆவணம்) கீழ் எஃப்.ஐ.ஆர் (FIR) பதிவு செய்யவும். (2) அசல் ஆவணம் மற்றும் தகவல் பரிமாற்றங்களை பாதுகாக்கவும். (3) 30 நாட்களுக்குள் சட்டப்பூர்வ நோட்டீஸ் அனுப்பி ஒப்பந்தத்தை ரத்து செய்ய நடவடிக்கை எடுக்கவும்.

question: भारतीय न्याय संहिता 2023 में धोखाधड़ी की क्या धारा है?
answer: भारतीय न्याय संहिता (BNS) 2023 की धारा 318 धोखाधड़ी (Cheating) के अपराध से संबंधित है (जो पहले IPC 420 थी)। यदि कोई व्यक्ति किसी को धोखा देकर संपत्ति देने के लिए बेईमानी से प्रेरित करता है, तो उसे 7 वर्ष तक के कारावास और जुर्माने से दंडित किया जाएगा।

question: जीरो एफआईआर (Zero FIR) क्या है और इसे कैसे दर्ज कराएं?
answer: जीरो एफआईआर का मतलब है कि किसी भी संज्ञेय अपराध के लिए भारत के किसी भी पुलिस स्टेशन में एफआईआर दर्ज कराई जा सकती है, चाहे घटना कहीं भी हुई हो। BNSS धारा 173 के तहत पुलिस को तुरंत शून्य (0) नंबर पर शिकायत दर्ज करनी होगी और बाद में उचित अधिकार क्षेत्र वाले पुलिस स्टेशन को स्थानांतरित करना होगा।

question: जमीन रजिस्ट्री से पहले कौन-कौन से दस्तावेज जांचने चाहिए?
answer: जमीन खरीदने से पहले महत्वपूर्ण दस्तावेज: (1) मूल सेल डीड (Title Deed) और 30 साल का भार-मुक्त प्रमाण पत्र (Encumbrance Certificate - EC)। (2) राज्य राजस्व रिकॉर्ड में पटटा / खतौनी / जमाबंदी में मालिक का नाम। (3) भौतिक सर्वेक्षण संख्या (Survey/Khasra Number) और सीमाएं। (4) स्थानीय प्राधिकरण (RERA / नगर निगम) से लेआउट अनुमोदन और एनओसी।

question: नौकरी के अनुबंध में गैर-प्रतिस्पर्धा खंड (Non-Compete Clause) क्या कानूनी है?
answer: भारतीय अनुबंध अधिनियम 1872 की धारा 27 के तहत नौकरी छोड़ने के बाद कर्मचारी पर काम करने या व्यवसाय करने पर रोक लगाने वाला गैर-प्रतिस्पर्धा खंड (Non-Compete Clause) पूरी तरह से शून्य (Void) और गैर-कानूनी है। भारतीय अदालतें रोजगार समाप्ति के बाद ऐसे प्रतिबंधों को लागू नहीं करती हैं।
